stories.body:
Real Madrid forward was dropped by brands for comments Chinese media generally steered clear of outlining

I t’s been a bad start to the week for the Kylian Mbappé. The France forward missed out on joining the elite roster of Ballon d’Or winners and instead became the latest high-profile addition to a far less illustrious list – that of foreign brands and individuals charged with “hurting the feelings of the Chinese people”.

The saga began when a video of the Real Madrid player making light of a meme involving him and China’s former leader Mao Zedong began spreading.

Within hours Mbappé found himself condemned online, before being unceremoniously dropped by brands , then held responsible for state television suspending the entire top Spanish league from its schedule. On Tuesday Mbappé apologised – “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China ” – as did La Liga, which released a statement saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans”.

Foreign brands from Mercedes to Versace and celebrities from John Cena to Katy Perry have previously been sent to the sin bin for crossing China’s political lines on Tibet, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Mbappé’s case shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains in China 50 years after his death – to the extent that most Chinese coverage of the affair does not even mention what the footballer said.

In the video, Mbappé references a meme of himself and “a guy … I think he was a Chinese dictator”, before a composite image of Mbappé’s face on Mao’s body pops up. (Mbappé has been nicknamed “the dictator” since his time at Paris Saint-Germain, a joke referring to his perceived influence at the club.)

The football app Dongqiudi was among the first to release a statement condemning the “inappropriate remarks”, but said: “Because his comments were offensive to China and the Chinese people, we cannot translate them.” Chinese media have reported on reactions such as the brand desertions, and the China Football Association’s lodging of a “stern protest” with Real Madrid – who apologised on Wednesday “to the Chinese people for any offence caused” – but have generally steered clear of outlining Mbappé’s precise offence.

The topic was still trending on Chinese social media on Wednesday morning, with one hashtag relating to the superstar’s apology boasting more than 600m views. Some posts asked variations on a simple question: “What did he actually say?”

Manya Koetse, editor of the Eye on Digital China newsletter, said in a post on X: “Many netizens without a VPN are still left in the dark about why all the talk about boycotting Mbappé is actually happening.”

Still, many expressed anger at what was characterised as disrespect for, as well as a misunderstanding of, China’s history. “For the majority of the [Chinese] people, Mao was and is still not seen as negatively as it is believed in the west,” said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University.

Mao was the founding leader of modern China, but his legacy includes radical policies such as the Great Leap Forward, an industrialisation policy blamed for a famine that killed as many as 30 million people by some estimates.

The ruling Communist party (CCP) maintains Mao was a revolutionary hero, though after his death it acknowledged another extreme policy, the violent Cultural Revolution, was a “grave mistake”.

Gao said: “There has been intense tension between Mao hatred and Mao support among the Chinese themselves. This tension is even more keenly felt since the economy has slowed.”

after newsletter promotion

Some scholars have pointed to a resurgence of interest in Mao among younger Chinese, with a yearning for a time they regard as more idealistic and egalitarian – something the CCP is keen to keep in check.

Jennifer Pan, professor of communication at Stanford University, said the difficulty of doing independent social science surveys in the past decade meant “our understanding of what Chinese people actually think is weak”. Pan said: “Social media doesn’t fill that gap. It’s noisy, unrepresentative, and censored … What we see is that companies, platforms, broadcasters and the foreign ministry moved together quickly. Did this follow public anger, or did this produce public anger? Either is possible, and we can’t tell which came first.”

Whichever way round, the financial cost for Mbappé is the same. His face is a common sight on Chinese buses, in subways and in online ads, and his commercial deals could be worth “as much as $30m (£22.6m) per year”, said Mark Dreyer, author of Sporting Superpower, a book about China’s ambitions in the sector.

However, “as soon as someone else has decided you’ve crossed the line, it’s a race to who can cut ties quickest, who can be the most patriotic”, he said. “Then you have to kiss the ring – there really is no other way if you want to stay in the market.”

Mbappé’s and La Liga’s swift apologies suggest they are trying to avoid a fate like the NBA, whose lucrative pre-season matches were shut out of China for six years after the Houston Rockets’ then general manager Daryl Morey voiced support for Hong Kong pro-democracy protests in 2019.

La Liga may have better luck, with the state broadcaster CCTV saying it would listen to what Mbappé had to say, and “more importantly” watch what he does.

On Wednesday a foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said: “We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made.”

Dreyer said: “It doesn’t sound like it’s an instant ‘all is forgiven’. But it sounds like they’re going to be a little bit more, for want of a better word, reasonable.”

stories.title: Trump admin sues Utah to save Kalshi from the state's total ban on gambling
stories.summary: US agency has sued 10 states for trying to stop gambling on prediction markets.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
US agency has sued 10 states for trying to stop gambling on prediction markets.

The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets.

Utah, which prohibits gambling, sued Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events.

“Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”

Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against a lawsuit filed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

Trump admin claims sole authority

The CFTC “has filed a lawsuit against Utah to block the state’s efforts to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets using state laws,” the commission said yesterday . “The lawsuit follows Utah’s decision to file civil enforcement actions in state court against CFTC-regulated markets and other businesses. Utah’s effort to restrict the functioning of CFTC-registered exchanges obstructs Congress’s decision to federally preempt state law.”

If Utah can shut down Kalshi, that could spell trouble for Kalshi’s chief prediction-market rival, Polymarket, and for sports betting sites like DraftKings and FanDuel. DraftKings and FanDuel advertise availability in all US states via a mix of products , including prediction-market platforms in states like Utah. Both are registered with the CFTC.

The Utah attorney general’s office declined to comment today on the CFTC lawsuit. The CFTC previously filed lawsuits against Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Kentucky, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Rhode Island, and Wisconsin. The federal agency also filed briefs supporting Kalshi in appeals court cases.

“Utah seeks to shut down prediction markets across a wide variety of markets,” CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said. “Event contracts do not just serve hedging and investment purposes—they also provide the public with information about the outcome of future events. Congress entrusted the CFTC to be the federal regulator with sole responsibility to oversee these markets. As I’ve said before, the CFTC has the expertise and responsibility to defend its exclusive jurisdiction over commodity derivatives, and that’s exactly what we’ll do.”

The US Commodity Exchange Act (CEA) gives the CFTC authority to regulate swaps. The key legal questions being grappled with by courts throughout the US are whether event contracts offered by prediction markets qualify as swaps, and whether the CFTC jurisdiction over swaps preempts states from applying their gambling laws.

US sues in same court where Utah beat Kalshi

The CFTC is suing Utah in the same US district court that previously ruled in Utah’s favor. Kalshi sued Utah in February in an attempt to stop the state from bringing an enforcement action against the prediction market.

In August, US District Judge Robert Shelby granted Utah’s motion for summary judgment and denied Kalshi’s motion for a preliminary injunction. Shelby wrote , “[T]he court concludes the federal law relied upon by Kalshi does not preempt Utah’s ability to enforce its anti-gambling laws.”

Shelby determined the text of US law makes it clear that state regulation is not forbidden. US law states that CFTC jurisdiction does not “supersede or limit the jurisdiction conferred on courts of the United States or any State,” and “explicitly provides for State regulation of its gaming laws in all but a few specified cases,” he wrote.

“Congress is aware that some States permit gambling while others do not, and the CEA explicitly provides for State jurisdiction,” Shelby wrote.

Most states in US want Supreme Court to rule

Kalshi is now appealing its loss to the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit but was unable to obtain an injunction preventing enforcement of the state gambling ban while that litigation continues. On September 8, Tenth Circuit judges denied Kalshi’s emergency motion for an injunction pending appeal. Utah filed its lawsuit seeking a shutdown of Kalshi about six weeks later.

The CFTC lawsuit against Utah makes arguments similar to the ones already rejected by the district court, although some other courts have ruled otherwise.

“Utah is not the first State that has attempted to invade the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction over swaps,” the CFTC lawsuit said. “Already, several federal courts—including the Third Circuit—have swiftly responded by issuing or affirming temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions barring the States from enforcing their gambling laws against CFTC-regulated exchanges that offer sports-related or other event contracts.”

The Third Circuit appeals court ruled that New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets. But Kalshi lost similar cases in the Sixth Circuit and Ninth Circuit in rulings that went in favor of Ohio, Tennessee, and Nevada.

Because circuit appeals courts are divided on the issue, it is likely that the Supreme Court will take up the case and determine whether states can apply their gambling laws to prediction markets. New Jersey petitioned the Supreme Court to resolve the circuit split, and 39 other states and the District of Columbia filed a brief supporting New Jersey’s petition.

stories.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
stories.summary: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 27 October 2026

Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.

Official data released in the last week , external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.

The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.

The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.

China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children .

The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.

At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.

No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.

The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.

"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.

The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.

Birth rates in China have been falling for years now

China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy , which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.

The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.

The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.

But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.

Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.

Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.

Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.

The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.

The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.

Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.

It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

stories.body:
OBR cautions about Middle East war dragging down growth and triggering a fresh cost of living crisis

Healey offers £100 payment to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

Budget 2026 live – latest updates

British households face a “grim picture” for living standards as the war in the Middle East drags down growth and triggers a fresh cost of living crisis, the government’s independent forecaster has said.

As John Healey announced his first budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) issued its report showing a sharp downgrade for growth in 2027, household disposable incomes and the public finances, despite the measures taken by the chancellor .

Although Healey sought to cushion the blow through “breathing space” policies to help with soaring energy costs, the watchdog said household disposable incomes after taking account of inflation would fall by 0.6% next year. The downgrade - compared with the 0.6% increase in disposable incomes that the OBR was forecasting in March – was driven mainly by higher energy costs.

While forecasting a modest recovery from next year, the OBR warned that families were facing among the weakest decades for growth in real household disposable income on records dating back to the 1960s.

Setting the stage for a tough election run-up for Labour, the watchdog said disposable incomes in 2029, after taking account of inflation, were on track to be only 1% higher than in 2019 – before the onset of the Covid pandemic.

“It’s a pretty grim picture”, David Miles of the OBR said.

“If you go back to just before Covid, and take that as your base, where we are right now - seven years later, is virtually no growth in per person real household disposable income,” he said.

“That’s pretty unusual in the history of the UK.”

As the impact from Donald Trump’s war hits British households, businesses and the government finances, Healey said the exchequer was spending £14bn more on debt interest as the financial market fallout from the conflict pushes up borrowing costs for countries worldwide.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, the chancellor said he would allow a hit to his buffer against the government’s fiscal rules – while also announcing a temporary rise in tax on banks to fund his package of energy support.

He left £15bn of headroom against the main fiscal rule , which requires day-to-day spending to be matched by tax receipts in three years’ time – down from £23.6bn left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, in the spring.

As a consequence, the OBR said borrowing was poised to fall to about 2% of GDP in the medium term but at a slower near-term pace than previous plans.

after newsletter promotion

As the energy price shock rippling out from the Middle East hits households and businesses, the OBR said consumers would face inflation of 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March.

Healey made helping families with the cost of living a core focus of his first budget, including £100 in blanket payments for 20 million households at a cost to the exchequer of £2.6bn and a plan to abolish standing charges on gas bills .

However, with the fallout from the war steadily mounting, the OBR warned that Britain’s resilience to the conflict that had been recorded so far this year would begin to fizzle out.

While it upgrades its growth forecast for this year from 1.1% to 1.2% after an unexpectedly resilient performance fuelled by AI investment, it slashed its estimate for next year from 1.5% to 1%.

Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war, after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise.

Although saying he would never be complacent, Healey said there were “signs of resilience” in the economy as he highlighted that the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund had issued growth upgrades for the UK within recent months.

“There are real challenges ahead but Britain has beaten the forecasts this year, and with the action I am taking today I believe Britain can beat the forecasts again,” he said.

However, the economy is coming under mounting pressure from the energy price shock triggered by the war. Since the start of the US-Israeli led invasion of Iran at the end of February, which has throttled energy flows in the region, oil prices have risen from about $70 a barrel to more than $115, while gas prices have almost tripled.

With a tentative pause in the fighting while Trump prepares for crunch midterm elections, the OBR said the outlook for the economy, households and the UK public finances remained highly uncertain.

Suggesting there were “significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability”, it said that if energy prices were to rise to a higher and more sustained peak, government borrowing could be £17bn above the central forecast next year. However, a lower energy price path could reduce borrowing by £12bn.

stories.title: Dharshini David: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions still unanswered
stories.summary: The chancellor talked of charting a new course for Britain, but the impact of Iran war has limited his options.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
While earnings are rising, forecasters predict that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes

Published 28 October 2026, 17:32 GMT

John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.

It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.

While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.

The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.

Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.

But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.

Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%

However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.

The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.

As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.

And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.

So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.

The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance Published 4 hours ago

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published 4 hours ago

So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.

Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.

There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.

And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.

The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.

Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.

Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.

And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.

Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.

So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.

With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.

The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.

So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.

For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.

A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

stories.title: China’s snooping around Pacific undersea cables raises risks for Big Tech
stories.summary: US-owned trans-Pacific cables face growing risks from sabotage and China.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
US-owned trans-Pacific cables face growing risks from sabotage and China.

Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters.

Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation.

One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission , an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026.

Mapping the risks

The report authors created an interactive Trans-Pacific Cable Gray Zone Vulnerability Index that ranks the undersea cables considered most at risk and displays a map of their routes spanning the Pacific Ocean. Such an index could help identify which cables should get highest priority in terms of placing underwater sensors or setting up patrols to monitor for threats.

Risk factors used in the vulnerability index include the undersea depth of the cable routes, nearby shipping traffic, cable ownership, China’s exclusive economic zone and broader territorial claims , and whether each cable connects to Taiwan. Taiwan is considered a geopolitical hotspot as a self-governing island democracy that is also claimed by China, with the latter ramping up military maneuvers involving warships and aircraft around Taiwan in recent years.

The index suggests that the risk to cables is highest around Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines, partly because of China’s claim of sovereignty over Taiwan but also because subsea cables linking the region to the United States must pass through shallow water with busy shipping lanes.

Among the 10 trans-Pacific cables identified as being most at risk, several are still under development with significant ownership stakes from US companies. These include the TPU project, owned by Google, the ORCA cable, owned by Meta, and the E2A cable, co-owned by Verizon along with firms in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan. All three of these projects had risk scores in the top five.

The report authors warn that any serious disruption to a single trans-Pacific cable could “risk overwhelming current available capacity on direct routings between the United States, Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, forcing data onto slower, less direct routes.”

An even greater disruption involving multiple cables, potentially during a geopolitical crisis involving Taiwan, could “significantly reduce headroom and even overwhelm trans-Pacific capacity as a whole,” with communications between the United States and Indo-Pacific region having to reroute through other cables across the globe. That could have major economic consequences for Internet communications, cloud services, and financial trading.

Dual-use technologies and survey tracks

This comes as the world’s major powers continue to build up their fleets of military submarines and undersea drones, along with further developing and deploying dual-use technologies, like undersea cable cutters that could either be used for repair or sabotage.

China has also deployed a fleet of research vessels equipped with seabed-mapping technologies near trans-Pacific undersea cables, according to a separate report published in October 2026 by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a think tank based in Washington, DC.

The CSIS analysts found that China-flagged research ships stood out as outliers in the amount of time spent near subsea infrastructure. They analyzed the movements of more than 200 research ships from multiple nations between 2020 and 2025.

This pattern involving Chinese vessels stood out even when compared with the generally high activity of US and Russian research ships on the high seas. Several Chinese ships spent much of their time performing survey-style tracks near undersea cables rather than checking out regions known for undersea mineral deposits.

One of the most surprising findings involved the China-linked research vessel Ke Xue that made a journey to the Bering Sea between Russia and the United States. While likely checking out a US military base in the Aleutian Islands, the ship also began doing “survey-like movements” near a Russian government-owned cable called Polar Express.

That likely indicates China’s interest in mapping Russia’s subsea telecommunications infrastructure, even though China and Russia have maintained strong economic and military ties, according to the CSIS analysts.

Chinese-owned fishing boats and cargo vessels have been involved in several notable cable-cutting incidents in recent years, especially near Taiwan. One incident in 2025 led to the first case of Taiwan’s government convicting and sentencing a Chinese captain to three years in prison, after his ship dropped anchor and performed a zigzag pattern that damaged the Tai-Peng 3 cable linking Taiwan to the offshore islands of Penghu.

The broader threat

The Pacific is not the only region where undersea cables face growing danger. In recent years, both Russian- and Chinese-linked ships have been investigated for causing damage to subsea communications cables, power cables, and pipelines in the Baltic Sea. These incidents typically involved ships that dragged their anchors over unusually long periods of time.

On October 21, The Telegraph published an analysis showing more than 500 incidents involving Russia’s fleet of fishing boats loitering near crucial undersea cables connecting the UK to the rest of the world, with some vessels following the routes of the undersea cables. Reuters reporting also recently revealed that NATO countries had confronted Russian submarines that were practicing how to disable undersea cables using a new type of technology in Arctic waters near Norway earlier this year.

Meanwhile, Iran has repeatedly threatened to charge fees to US tech companies for the undersea Internet cables running beneath the contested Strait of Hormuz and has prepared plans to attack them —another consequence of the wider war that began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026.

For a big-picture perspective on why the world has become more dangerous for the Internet’s undersea backbone, Ars recently interviewed Elisabeth Braw , author of the book Undersea War .

This story was updated on October 28, 2026 with additional details about how a China-linked research vessel unexpectedly spent some time apparently surveying a Russian subsea cable.

stories.title: Victory! You Can Now Exclude Apps from Siri AI
stories.summary: In the most recent update to Apple’s devices, iOS 27.2, the company has introduced a new setting to “Exclude Apps” from Siri AI, fulfilling one of our asks from our Encrypt It Already campaign earlier this year . One of our main concerns with new AI features on devices is how those features interact with end-to-end encrypted content, particularly with secure messaging apps. Many AI features require cloud processing, and despite privacy protections engineered into these systems , the content of secure messaging apps may leave a user’s device without their knowledge. In the most recent update to Apple’s devices, iOS 27.2, the company has introduced a new setting to “Exclude Apps” from Siri AI, fulfilling one of our asks from our Encrypt It Already campaign earlier this year .

One of our main concerns with new AI features on devices is how those features interact with end-to-end encrypted content, particularly with secure messaging apps. Many AI features require cloud processing, and despite privacy protections engineered into these systems , the content of secure messaging apps may leave a user’s device without their knowledge. That changes the privacy concerns around using those tools. In a perfect world, users would be able to put a barrier up to ensure data from certain apps doesn’t leave the device. Here was our initial ask:

You should be able to tell the operating system’s AI to not access an app, even if that comes at the “cost” of missing out on some features. The setting should be straightforward and easy to understand in ways the Gemini and Apple Intelligence controls currently are not.

At launch, we found the settings to control Siri AI’s app access behavior pretty confusing . You had to toggle several options to block Siri AI off from accessing an app, or disable Siri AI entirely. Turning off Siri AI and reverting to Siri Classic is, for now, still a good option if you’d prefer to use the older version.

The most recent update is far more clear and does more to protect your data. And, just as expected, it comes at the cost of some features. That’s a good thing, actually. The features not working shows that the new setting is effective.

Here’s how to add apps to the exclusion list, once you’ve updated to 27.2:

Open Settings > Siri > Excluded Apps

Tap “Add Apps” and select any apps you’d like to add to the exclusion list

Now Siri AI cannot access the contents of the app. Excluding an app also means you may lose some features. For example, if you exclude the Apple Messages app, you will no longer be able to have Siri AI read or respond to messages for you. Even the “onscreen awareness” feature, where you invoke Siri and ask it for information about what you’re currently looking at, will not work anymore. For example, if you exclude Signal, you cannot invoke Siri and ask it to discern any information in the Signal app. You’ll just get these messages:

Tap your user photo, then Settings > Personal Intelligence > Connected Apps

Revoke access to any apps you do not want Gemini to have access to

stories.title: Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
stories.summary: The chancellor targets the cost of living amid global economic turmoil but opposition parties say he has not been bold enough.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 28 October 2026, 18:11 GMT

Millions of households will get £100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, John Healey has announced in his first Budget.

The chancellor said he wanted to give hard-pressed families "breathing space now" and "hope for the future" as the UK economy is battered by "global economic storms".

He also unveiled tax breaks to boost high street businesses - but confirmed that many big decisions, including on defence spending and welfare, will not be made until next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Healey's plans were "not bold enough" and the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".

In an hour-long speech to a packed House of Commons, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other frontbench colleagues cheering him on, the chancellor unveiled a string of measures aimed at cutting the cost of living.

These include:

One-off £100 energy payment for people living in council tax bands A to D in England, with Wales saying it will match the payment and the Scottish government planning to "replicate" it

Gas standing charges in England, Scotland and Wales, to be scrapped during 2027 "or as soon as possible after". These fixed daily fees will be shifted onto the price of each unit of energy, meaning heavy gas users will face higher bills

Extending the 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel to July

Increasing minimum wage rates by 3.9% in April, although there will be no progress on narrowing the gap between rates for older and younger workers

Healey increased the tax on the profits of big banks from 3% to 6%, which will last from January next year to April 2028, and increased taxes on high-stakes gambling machines.

Healey announces £100 energy bill help for millions and raises taxes on banks and some savers

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance Published 4 hours ago

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published 4 hours ago

Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures Published 4 hours ago

As part of a package to help business, Healey increased the point at which High Street shops in England start paying business rates from £12,000 to £18,000, with vape shops and adult gaming centres excluded from the relief.

But he had little scope for big giveaways as the public finances remain stretched, with the UK set to spend £14bn more on debt interest payments this year.

Income tax thresholds will remain frozen and the tax on income from savings and property rental will rise to 24% for basic rate taxpayers from April 2027, after it had been scheduled to go up to 22%.

But a cut to the cash ISA allowance from £20,000 a year to £12,000, announced last year by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, will be axed.

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded its growth forecast for next year to 1%, with slightly higher increases predicted for subsequent years.

In its latest assessment, the OBR said British households were set to be little better off than before the Covid pandemic even a decade after Covid-19 hit, a situation the watchdog's boss David Miles described as "pretty grim".

In his Budget speech, Healey repeatedly stressed that the UK economy was being battered by "global uncertainties" and soaring oil prices caused by conflict in the Middle East.

"Those are the storms we face. We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them," he told MPs.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: What are the key points from the Budget and how will it be funded?

Healey also used his speech to announce plans to allow regional mayors to keep 20% of business rates and a share of income tax to spend on local priorities.

The aim was to allow mayors to retain 100% of business rates raised in their areas by the end of the decade, he added, in "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".

And he sought to address opposition claims the Labour government is unwilling to cut benefits, insisting that both he and Burnham were committed to bringing down the welfare bill in a "Labour way".

But he said no decisions would be taken until reviews by Alan Milburn , into young people not in work or training, and Stephen Timms, on Personal Independence Payments , had been published, with legislation to follow next year.

The £4.7bn black hole in the defence investment plan will be funded, the chancellor revealed, in part through taking money from capital budgets across Whitehall.

Healey said he will set out how the government plans to meet its commitment to spend 3% of the national income on defence by 2030, and 3.5% by 2035, at next year's spending review.

But Badenoch said he "should have set out a plan for 3% today," highlighting his claim when he resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June that UK forces were at risk due to a lack of cash.

"So now he is the man who is increasing risk to personnel on operations, he is the man who is making our country less safe, he has failed his own test," the Conservative leader said.

"This is on him and no-one will ever forget. If he had any decency he would resign again today."

The Tory leader said that with the UK heading for a record tax burden and "spending more on debt interest than on the army and schools combined", Healey's Budget was "not good enough, not strong enough, not bold enough".

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the Budget "has a raft of fiddly measures but very little that will move the dial on growth".

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said that until the government has "the courage" to fix the UK's trading relationship with the EU any Budget will just be "tinkering around the edges" and will not provide the growth the country needs.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the Budget was full of "little giveaways" but "doesn't overall do very much" and did not offer "anything of any value on defence whatsoever".

Healey also faced criticism from the left, with the general secretary of the Unite union, Sharon Graham describing the cost of living measures in the Budget as "baby steps".

"Scrapping standing charges on gas and a £100 energy payment for households in council tax bands, A to D, whilst welcome, will not touch the sides, when many forecasts show bills set to jump over £400 in January," she added.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was a Budget "that betrays the future for young people and the planet they inherit".

He added: "The chancellor didn't mention climate once but praised bankers repeatedly."

Video appears to show Mao Zedong called a ‘dictator’

Dongpeng and Mengniu end deals with the player

Kylian Mbappé has apologised after the Real Madrid forward was dropped by major Chinese brands for apparently joking about Mao Zedong in a video that has gone viral. There were also signs of broader repercussions, with the state-run Chinese digital newspaper The Paper reporting that public television was suspending broadcasts of matches from La Liga.

The offending video shows Mbappé saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen involving him was of his face photoshopped on to that of “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappé superimposed on an image of Mao.

“My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone my words have upset,” Mbappé said in a statement in French, Chinese and English.

Spain’s La Liga also apologised, saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent La Liga.” In China, jokes about Mao, the country’s founding leader who died in 1976 – and whose drastic policies are also blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths – remain taboo.

The beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year’s World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappé consuming its sport drink, said it was terminating all cooperation with the France captain. “Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments,” Dongpeng said in a statement.

Mengniu, China’s largest dairy producer, and cheese maker Milkground also said that they were cutting ties with Mbappé, who until now was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of social media followers. “Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappé” was the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo with 430m views.

One Weibo user said the “extremely serious wrong remarks … crossed the red line” and others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappé’s image from their bottles. Dongqiudi, one of China’s biggest online football outlets, said Mbappé’s remarks were “offensive to China and the Chinese people”.

In an interview with the French sports newspaper L’Equipe last month, the 27-year-old Mbappé addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator. “There’s a part of it that’s funny … but there is another part that’s a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history,” he said.

China’s foreign ministry said it was aware of the reports regarding Mbappé, who on Monday finished runner-up to Harry Kane in the Ballon d’Or award for the world’s best player. “Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with unanimous rejection from all sectors of Chinese society,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing.

after newsletter promotion

The Paper cited sources at the state broadcaster saying that CCTV has suspended all broadcasts of La Liga matches, and removed all advertisements involving Mbappé. On the CCTV website, La Liga matches this weekend were still on its online viewing schedule.

Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors there. The former NBA player Dwight Howard referred to Taiwan as a country in 2023 as he appeared in a video with the island’s then vice-president and current president, Lai Ching-te, sparking fury on Chinese social media. Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.

The Houston Rockets general manager, Daryl Morey, posted a tweet in 2019 supporting Hong Kong protests, leading to China suspending sponsorship deals with the NBA and pulling games off Chinese television for a year.

Fans in China made their feelings clear. “I used to really enjoy watching Mbappé play on the pitch,” Zhang Jingqi, 30, who works at a mall in Beijing, said. “But ever since this news broke yesterday I have lost that admiration, sorry to say.”

stories.title: Court Should Curb Abuse of Grand Jury Subpoenas Targeting Social Media Users
stories.summary: A federal appeals court should curb the government’s abuse of grand jury subpoenas to unmask social media users who criticize lawless immigration enforcement. That is the message from the ACLU, EFF, and other civil liberties and trade groups who filed a friend-of-the-court brief in a sealed case in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. The case involves the government’s investigation of an anonymous Reddit user who commented on a post about an immigration officer in Minnesota. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) first issued an administrative subpoena to Reddit to unmask the user. When the user challenged the subpoena in court on free speech and statutory grounds ( as many others have ), DHS withdrew it. But then the government obtained a separate grand jury subpoena—a subpoena issued by a prosecutor to gather evidence to present to a grand jury before any criminal charges are filed—for much of the same information. The user then challenged the grand jury subpoena too, and the case is currently being appealed. The right to speak anonymously is essential. It preserves privacy and shields critics from government retaliation. In the past year, the Department of Justice (DOJ) has issued grand jury subpoenas to social media companies for their users’ personal data. This is frequently done for improper purposes and without really showing that social media users have committed any crime. These subpoenas have the effect of intimidating and chilling critics, as immigration authorities have engaged in invasive , unconstitutional , and sometimes violent conduct . As the amicus brief makes clear, courts should not defer to the government’s claims regarding the legitimacy of using grand jury subpoenas to unmask internet users. Instead, the subpoenas must receive proper First Amendment scrutiny. Like many other types of legal processes, grand jury subpoenas are issued by federal officials without prior court approval. And they too can be abused to harass or retaliate against people critical of the government. The amicus brief was filed in early September and recently unsealed. The brief was signed by the American Civil Liberties Union of DC, EFF, the Center for Individual Rights, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, the Cato Institute, and NetChoice. stories.title: Social media is full of weird video game mashups. Where are they all coming from?
stories.summary: AI tools are making it easier to modify and recreate games, raising questions about piracy, copyright and how far the technology could disrupt the industry • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here If your social media algorithms have clocked that you’re into video games, something strange will have happened in the past few weeks. Your feed, like mine, will have been full of clips of streamers playing bizarre mashups of popular video games . Skyrim in Minecraft. Halo, except the main character is Mario. Skate 2 in Call of Duty maps. A flood of professional-looking fan-coded game mods that are mildly interesting to look at for 30 seconds, but ultimately inconsequential. Would I download a mod that lets me play Wii Bowling inside a zombie shooter? No, but I am very interested in where they came from. Of course, the answer – or at least, most of the answer – is AI. After a week of researching this (thanks especially to Replay Mode on YouTube for this informative video , which set me down this track) I now understand that these mashup mods are not just AI-generated videos, but AI-assisted coding. Basically, as of a few weeks ago, Anthropic’s Claude has become extremely good at decompiling video game code. Games are written by humans in readable code and then compiled into binary 1s and 0s that the PC or console running it can read; decompiling is the reversal of that process, revealing a game’s source code, which humans can then edit and mess around with for fun. This used to be an extremely laborious process. But now it is not, because humans aren’t doing much of it any more. Continue reading...

Payments to 20m homes part of package to cut energy bills and ease cost of living crisis, paid for by bank windfall tax

‘A pretty grim picture’: outlook for UK living standards slashed despite Healey’s budget

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

John Healey promised to steer Britain through “global economic storms” as he announced an energy giveaway of £100 to 80% of households in England, funded by a smaller than expected windfall tax on banks.

In his first budget, the chancellor said 20 million households in council tax bands A to D would receive a £100 payment – a measure he said would cost £2.6bn.

That includes equivalent funding for Scotland and Wales, whose governments can decide whether to replicate the measure. The policy will help a large number of middle earners, reaching houses worth up to about £600,000 in London.

“I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space,” he said, announcing the payment.

The relief on bills comes at a cost to big banks via the banking surcharge rise, and to savers and landlords, who were hit with an unexpected tax rise.

Healey said his budget would shape Britain’s future on defence, energy, welfare and entrepreneurship. “This Labour government has set a course for fresh hope, good growth and support for those who need it.”

The chancellor also extended the VAT cut on electricity bills until next July, and as widely expected, cancelled fuel duty rises pencilled in by Rachel Reeves.

Healey said this would help businesses as well as consumers. “For millions of people, the cost of living and the cost of doing business are the same. The home is the office. The van is the family car,” he said.

He blamed the war in the Middle East for the deterioration in the economic outlook since Reeves’s spring statement, but insisted he would keep Labour’s deficit-reduction plans on track.

“Analysts like to speak of economic headwinds, but what we face today are global economic storms,” he said, describing his statement as “a budget built on fiscal discipline, which matches immediate action today with clear direction for the future”.

He said higher inflation as a result of the Iran war was expected to cost the government £14bn more in interest costs and the Office for Budget Responsibility had downgraded its growth forecast to 1% for next year, from the 1.6% it expected in the spring.

Healey nevertheless promised to meet Labour’s first fiscal rule, on balancing current spending with tax receipts by 2029-30, but with diminished headroom of £15bn – against the £24bn that Reeves set aside in March. He said the cushion would be rebuilt to £22bn by 2030-31. “That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can.”

The chancellor said the energy package would be funded by a windfall tax on Britain’s banks and the unexpected two percentage-point income tax rise for landlords and savers.

after newsletter promotion

He is doubling the additional levy the banks pay on their profits to 6% from the current 3% for 15 months from January. That fell short of the rise to 8% that many industry figures had expected.

Healey lavished praise on the sector as he announced the measure. “I want to say directly to our banks: I celebrate and I am grateful for the role that you play,” he said. Bank share prices rose after the announcement, with NatWest and Standard Chartered up by more than 4%.

Healey announced several measures intended to cut businesses’ costs – including raising the rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for companies in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. The change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops, he said.

There was a package of policies that Healey said would tackle the “moral mission” of homelessness.

There will be no easing of fiscal drag, however, despite Andy Burnham previously expressing concern at the rate at which households were being pulled into higher rates of income tax.

Forecasts show that the freeze on tax thresholds will drag an extra 6.7m people into paying income tax and push 5.4m more into the higher rate band by 2031–32. The minimum wage will increase by 3.9% to £13.21 an hour, an increase of £910 to the gross annual earnings of a full-time worker.

Pensions will also rise thanks to the triple lock, but with new tax relief to keep pensioners from paying income tax as the state pension rises above the personal allowance for the first time. About 500,000 pensioners are to benefit.

Healey also announced sweeping new powers for regions, pledging all mayors would be given a share of income tax revenue from 2028. He said he intended that local and regional government would retain 100% of business rates income before the end of the decade.

He said the devolution package would be “new powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics”.

stories.body:
It was a “breathing space” budget from Chancellor John Healey. In the absence of big surprises or bold change, Healey’s trade-off appears to be small reliefs now in exchange for “fresh hope” in the future. Here’s what our experts made of the chancellor’s first budget.

Targeted help with energy costs as bills keep rising

Jonquil Lowe, Visiting Academic, The Open University

This budget took place against a backdrop of global turmoil and rising inflation, driven largely by higher energy costs. These are continuing to squeeze household budgets. From January, the energy price cap is predicted to rise by 27% to nearly £2,200 a year for a typical household.

Help with energy costs is therefore an important move. This support includes a £100 energy payment for households in England in council tax bands A to D (the devolved governments will receive equivalent funding to replicate this).

There was also a commitment to abolish the standing charge for gas (currently on average 30 pence a day ). The amount will instead be added to the charge for the unit cost of each kilowatt-hour used. This gives households more control over their bills – it will mean that limiting the amount of gas they use will have a bigger effect on reducing their cost. However, one worry is that squeezed households could still risk their health by not heating their homes adequately.

Labour’s manifesto pledged not to raise taxes on working people. This budget technically kept to that if we assume that working people just receive earnings. But building on last year’s changes, this budget has introduced another increase to the tax rates on interest from savings and rental income. Landlords and some savers will be taxed at a basic rate of 24% (currently 20%), higher rate 44% (from 40%) and additional rate 49% (from 45%) from April 2027.

This makes it all the more welcome that a proposal last year to cut the cash ISA limit for savers aged under 65 to £12,000 is being abandoned. Everyone, regardless of their age, will still be able to put up to £20,000 a year into a cash ISA (or cash and money funds within a stocks-and-shares ISA) and receive the interest tax-free.

The government will also consult on setting up a first-time buyer ISA to replace the Lifetime ISA and help people save for a home. From February 2027, a new scheme called Your First Home will provide equity loans for first-time buyers purchasing new properties. The loan, worth 20% of the purchase price, will be tax-free for the first five years. To be eligible buyers must have a household income of no more than £110,000 (£140,000 in London).

Read more: It’s not just rough sleeping – Andy Burnham’s housing plans need to include the ‘hidden homeless’

The budget also delivered a higher tax-free personal allowance for pensioners on the lowest incomes. The new Pension Tax Allowance will be applied automatically, with HMRC doing the sums. Pensioners with income up to £13,037 (the full state pension) will pay no income tax from April 2027. For comparison, for younger people the standard allowance is frozen at £12,570 until April 2031. They would pay £93.40 tax on an income of £13,037.

The announcements come on top of a drip feed of “everyday fixes” in the days leading up to the budget. These included reform of carer’s allowance so that carers no longer lose their whole allowance of £86.45 a week once their earnings pass a weekly limit of £204. But it has already emerged that this much-touted change will not come into effect until 2030 while the government updates its IT systems.

Small clues that this government is chasing growth

Maha Rafi Atal, Adam Smith Senior Lecturer in Political Economy, University of Glasgow

For years, the UK has faced a structural deadlock: a public that demands robust state services, but which rejects both the broad-based income taxes and pro-growth measures like increased immigration that might fund those services. Under Rachel Reeves’ chancellorship, Labour tried to get around this by raising the necessary taxes indirectly – from everywhere but income. This made it more expensive for businesses to operate, failing to jumpstart growth.

In this budget, John Healey has tried a different tack, deploying selective business reliefs alongside a commitment to increased defence spending. Together, these measures make a calculated gamble that state stimulus can rescue the economy from lacklustre growth. In a growing economy, the government gets more tax revenue to fund services even without raising rates, because there’s more economic activity to tax in the first place.

The reliefs for business are welcome. Raising the small business rate relief threshold – effectively removing half of all shops, restaurants and gyms from the rates system – provides breathing room for local economies. When paired with the electricity bill reduction for core industries and the introduction of “founders’ relief” for entrepreneurs selling shares in their business, the budget offers some incentives for corporate investment and entrepreneurial risk.

The chancellor has also listened in part to businesses that complained of rising costs as a result of the increase in employers’ national insurance and the new measures in the Employment Rights Act . While the minimum wage is set to rise, the government has restored a lower rate for younger workers. This will benefit some businesses in employing people more cheaply, but the government also hopes it will help absorb school-leavers and graduates into the workforce, increasing productivity and reducing the welfare bill.

The budget introduces two distinct avenues for the state to proactively stimulate growth. First, through accelerated defence commitments (spending 3% of GDP by 2030, for example), the chancellor is injecting capital directly into domestic supply chains, manufacturing, and high-tech engineering. Second, the roadmap for fiscal devolution offers a regional stimulus by promising to let mayors keep 100% of local business rates by the end of the decade, as well as a share of income tax receipts. This kind of arrangement, to fund infrastructure and attract business, is standard practice in most federalised systems. But its absence has been an unusual quirk of UK devolution.

Yet, while these measures are constructive, it is not clear that they are enough to reverse the grim reality: growth is stagnant at just over 1% and the Office for Budget Responsibility predicts it will stay that way.

Unlike its predecessor, this government seems to accept that it desperately needs some growth, and therefore some private investment, or public services will fall apart. In this budget, it has signaled some understanding that it may have to meet business halfway to get there. But the fiscal forecast relies on the hope that these stimuli will take effect in time to expand the tax base and preserve public spending before the next election.

If they do not, the Treasury has also signaled that like Reeves before him, Healey will resort to spending cuts in the final years of the parliament to balance the books. By deferring that choice, the government has chosen to pray for a growth miracle today, while keeping the threat of real-terms austerity on the horizon tomorrow.

Banks to pay more – but Healey bids to keep them lending

Alper Kara, Professor of Banking and Finance, Brunel University of London

One surprise is the relatively modest increase in taxes on banks compared with what financial markets had been expecting. There had been speculation that the government would raise the surcharge on bank profits from 3% to 8%. Instead, the surcharge will increase to 6% for just 15 months, from January 2027. So banks will face a higher tax bill, but a smaller one than many investors had feared.

Shares in some major UK banks rose as investors welcomed the smaller-than-expected increase. This suggests that investors believe the profitability of banks will be less affected by the tax increase than previously feared.

But the decision also reflects the difficult balance facing the chancellor. The government needs more money to support public spending and manage its finances, particularly at a time when borrowing costs remain high . Banks are an attractive source of revenue because their profits have been relatively strong in recent years.

And since 2023, higher interest rates have helped many banks earn more. These profits come from the difference between what banks charge borrowers and what they pay savers. So, the government has a reasonable argument that banks should make a greater contribution to public finances. This is especially true when households and businesses have been struggling with high living costs.

However, the amount of additional revenue matters. Taxing banks more will generate £1.5 billion in extra income for the Treasury, but it is unlikely to make a substantial difference to the government’s wider spending commitments, such as defence. A temporary increase also means that the additional revenue cannot be relied upon over the longer term.

And the next question is who will ultimately pay for this tax increase. Banks could absorb the additional cost through lower profits and reduced returns to shareholders. Alternatively, they might try to protect their profitability by offering lower savings rates, charging higher interest rates on new mortgages and business loans, or increasing fees for customers.

However, competition in the banking market will limit how much of the tax banks can pass on to customers. Banks that increase mortgage rates or reduce savings rates risk losing customers to competitors. Given that the surcharge increase will last only 15 months, my view is that banks may prefer to absorb much of the additional cost rather than risk losing market share.

The chancellor’s decision to keep the annual cash ISA allowance at £20,000, rather than reducing it to £12,000 as previously planned could also help banks. Cash ISA deposits are an important source of funding for banks and building societies, particularly for mortgage lending.

Keeping the higher allowance could help banks retain those deposits and avoid additional funding pressures. This may also be part of the chancellor’s attempt to balance higher bank taxes with the need to keep banks lending to households and businesses.

There are also wider considerations. Higher taxes could affect the international competitiveness of the UK banking sector, as banks consider taxation when deciding where to expand their operations. Sustained higher taxation could discourage investment in the UK banking sector, potentially leading to fewer new jobs or even job losses over the longer term.

By opting for a smaller and temporary increase, the chancellor appears to have recognised these risks. His decision seems to be aimed at a balance between raising additional revenue and limiting the impact on lending and investment.

Relief on energy bills could remove push for heat pumps

Dylan Ryan, Lecturer in Mechanical & Energy Engineering, Edinburgh Napier University

The overall cost of heating with gas will drop for most people , except for those with larger homes, after the chancellor’s announcement.

Once the standing charge, a fixed daily fee, is removed, gas bills will reflect what people actually use. While these lower-than-expected bills will be a welcome relief for bill payers, it could weaken the economic case for households to switch to using heat pumps.

There had been rumours of cuts to the boiler upgrade scheme intended to help more home owners install heat pumps. However, that didn’t happen. A government report on the scheme said that 65% of property owners who installed heat pumps did so because this grant was available. The report also pointed out that 52% of all recipients of the grant were large detached four-bedroom or bigger homes. So, some sort of reform could be needed.

The cut to VAT on electricity and the £100 paid to those in bands A-D homes will also provide some relief for energy bill-payers.

However, energy prices are expected to rise again by the next price cap adjustment in January 2027, due to the Iran war pushing up global energy prices. The government may need to provide some additional relief then. For example, further decoupling electricity prices from the price of gas , as gas often sets the price for electricity.

Ultimately, moving energy use away from fossil fuels is a balancing act. But the government is going to have to make further changes if it expects to meet its climate change targets by 2050.

Teenagers in England will be able to take GCSEs in vocational subjects – that could include digital tech and building and construction – from September 2029. These qualifications will be taken in schools by 14-16-year-olds, with the subjects decided in consultation with regional and local leaders . The new policy also includes a requirement for work experience, which has not been compulsory for under-16s since 2012 .

But the broadening of the curriculum to allow for vocational qualifications from the age of 14 is not new. Technical Awards are currently offered by nine in ten schools with similar subjects to those suggested for vocational GCSEs. Technical awards are designed explicitly for 14-16 year olds to undertake applied study of a sector or broad occupational group, such as leisure, travel and tourism . Assessment must include an exam that makes up at least 40% of the overall mark. The resulting qualification counts in performance tables as equivalent to one GCSE .

The government’s new proposals differ from the current system because the content for the vocational GCSEs will be set nationally. Content for existing Technical Awards is set by awarding organisations. The decision about which vocational GCSEs will be offered in an area will be led by local areas themselves.

These differences, alongside the requirement for work experience, signal a clearer link to the local labour market. In addition, content being set at a national level could mean that it is more aligned with occupational standards . These are profiles that describe the knowledge, skills and behaviours needed to be competent in a particular occupation.

This alignment could allow young people to better understand the vocational options available to them from 16. They will have had the opportunity to learn about broader occupations through one or more vocational GCSEs with effective practical learning, and had some work experience from 14.

Existing options

While a renewed focus on technical education is always welcome, there have been several attempts to provide high status vocational options for young people from age 14. The Tomlinson Review in 2004 made the case for a 14-19 diploma where academic and technical learning would be combined in a single qualification with different levels and lines of specialism. However, this did not sufficiently convince politicians to scrap GCSEs and A Levels.

Academics Ann Hodgson and Ken Spours wrote frequently in the 2000s about the need for a 14-19 upper secondary phase in England, including both vocational and academic programmes. From 2003 to 2009, social issues charity the Nuffield Foundation carried out a substantial review on 14-19 education, which called for the “re-assertion of a broader vision of education”.

The free market approach to education policy under the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government allowed for the establishment of University Technical Colleges (UTCs), introduced in 2010. UTCs were an attempt to create upper secondary institutions for 14-19 year olds focused on technical subjects in England. They faced challenges of recruiting learners at 14 and maintaining employer links, yet over 40 still remain across England and they show good destination outcomes for those who start at a UTC aged 16.

During this period, vocational courses for 14-year-olds in colleges were also developed. Although not widespread, it has been possible to study at a college as a 14-year-old since 1992 , with a more formal system in existence since the mid 2010s . These courses are generally taken at colleges alongside the remainder of learning at school, although 14-16-year-olds can now be full-time at a college.

Research from 2007 suggests that young people wanted to study in a different way when they selected a vocational option at a college. Colleges have resources for vocational subjects that are not available to schools, both in terms of equipment used for post-16 vocational courses, and specialist vocational teachers.

Technical Awards were introduced in schools in 2014. Regulations around assessment were tightened in 2020.

Recent figures suggest around 45% of young people take a Technical Award at school. A small cohort of young people attend further education colleges from age 14, accessing industry standard equipment and a different kind of learning. Progression rates are good, with 75% or more moving into post-16 education.

Technical progression

There is now an established high-status technical route for young people aged 16-18 in the form of a T-level, introduced in 2020. These are technical qualifications for post 16-education that are the equivalent of three A-levels, and include a significant work placement, while being related to occupational standards. This has been a key change in the system, and although numbers are currently small , expansion is planned .

Further reforms announced in 2025 to vocational qualifications for those over 16 also signify a major shift. Learners will be able to pick up to three vocational subjects to study for V-levels, each equivalent to one A-level. Their peers studying at level two – qualifications taken after the age of 16 but the equivalent academic level to GCSEs – can study for an Occupational Certificate over two years, then move directly into work , or study for a Foundation Certificate then progress to A-, T- or V-levels.

Combined with these changes, the vocational GCSEs announcement offers the potential for more young people to experience different vocational subjects as well as some work experience from the age of 14. This could enable them to make more informed decisions about their post-16 options.

The current system and the reforms to post-16 vocational qualifications mean that any technical pathways are, and will remain, less rigid in England than in countries which sort young people into different kinds of school for upper secondary education.

A greater understanding of the different types of work will help young people who ultimately transition to vocational learning post-16. However, the changes from age 14 rely on schools having the appropriate resources to make that vocational learning meaningful.
