stories.title: Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law
stories.summary: The post Turbulent Times Call For Experimental Law appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Experiments with the rule of law around the world are creating the kind of resiliency we need in our era of uncertainty.

MUNICH — Shortly after wandering into the Munich Urban Colab this summer, I found myself trying to follow an intense conversation in German about the city’s new experiment with autonomous buses. A local official, clocking my curious puzzlement, offered an aside in English: “We are asking ourselves: ‘What does it mean when the law is an experiment too?’”

No question may be more essential to governance in our era of dangerous uncertainty.

Global warming is accelerating faster than global treaties on mitigation can be negotiated. Climate catastrophes occur with a sudden ferocity beyond what current adaptation laws anticipate. Biological threats surface and kill before public health responses can be formulated. And AI is evolving faster and more wildly than regulators or lawmakers, or even its designers, expect.

All this dizzying unpredictability is undermining traditional legal structures. The threat is not just to the rule of law, but to the very nature of law, at least as humans have conceived it.

Our societies have long considered the law a slow and steady force, “the essential foundation of stability and order” in the words of J. William Fulbright. To that end, law is backward-looking — “the government of the living by the dead,” according to Oliver Wendell Holmes. The lawmaking process in republics and democracies is age-old: observe a problem, study its particularities, debate solutions and then carve out a rule that will endure for years or decades.

But what happens when the future arrives faster than your regional regulator or local parliament can make a rule?

The emerging answer is experimental law or, in Germany, where Munich is a hotbed, Experimentierklauseln . “Experimental clauses” refer to sections and parts of laws that are made flexible, often for set time periods, to allow for real-time adaptation or alteration in response to changing threats, climate or technology.

The shift toward such experimentation has begun, albeit slowly, in only certain areas of the law. Contract law and administrative law, especially where they touch on technology or other advanced sectors of the economy, are becoming more fluid.

Contracts, once used to protect against all contingencies, are now written more openly — explicitly anticipating new knowledge and adjustments. Among startups and innovation-oriented companies, written agreements are less likely to specify payments for specific work at specific times and more likely to establish processes for collaboration and shared decision-making.

For example, start-ups use Agile contracts with vendors that, instead of pledging a final digital product at a price, set parameters of a creative process involving a test phase, iterative feedback loops and product benchmarks. Biotech startups rely on a “relational contract” with manufacturers to create a collaboration framework that includes regular meetings, shared lab notes and a commitment to use best efforts to scale a prototype.

Meanwhile, smart contracts have become commonplace in supply chains to allow for real-time changes in inventory levels. Union contracts in digital workplaces often incorporate adaptive provisions — “continuous bargaining” in 21st-century labor parlance — with guidelines for how workers participate across the lifecycles of systems and products.

Modern tech procurement uses what’s called “Dynamic Service Level Agreements” that feature automatic updates, scalable license adjustments, and continuous remote monitoring and interventions by seller and buyer. “Data Processing Agreements” within cloud contracts dynamically adjust data handling and security protocols as privacy regulations and digital risks shift. In some cases, AI agents have written contracts in code rather than in English. Put simply, some contracts now write themselves.

Similarly, regulatory agencies and public administrations have moved away from the time-consuming traditional rulemaking process, since rules quickly become outdated in a world so strange and fast-changing. Instead, agencies and administrative judges, particularly in advanced economies, are more likely to offer “guidance” — advisories, memos, letters or protocols that are regularly tweaked or edited in response to updated knowledge and changing circumstances.

These shifts point toward an emerging and quite radical recognition, especially in law, that extreme uncertainty is not a problem to be solved, but a reality and even an ally. The fact that the future is too hard for anyone to know is leveling. The regulator, the regulated and the everyday person all know the same thing: almost nothing.

The act of lawmaking then becomes a great collaboration between governments and experts and firms and workers and the regular people most affected. And that collaboration is a search, never-ending, for improvements and innovations and solutions.

Such collaboration turns lawmaking as we know it on its head. Implementation is required first to understand what the policy should be. In this new paradigm, resilience is grounded in fragility. Resilience does not come from buffering organizations against known risks, but by designing them to show quickly when they are broken, so they can be reconfigured. It is a kind of deliberately induced and carefully controlled institutional fragility. Strain is immediately apparent, triggering investigation and countermeasures well before it ramifies into catastrophe.

“Experimental clauses allow for real-time adaptation in response to changing threats, climate or technology.”

Climate Changes The Law

The stakes of achieving this new, more open mentality are expressed perhaps most clearly in our response to global warming. In the 2022 book, “Fixing the Climate: Strategies for an Uncertain World,” Columbia Law School’s Charles F. Sabel and UC San Diego’s David G. Victor argue that decades of top-down global climate diplomacy — from the Kyoto Protocol to the Paris Agreement — have failed because they rely on inflexible global treaties.

Treaties are among the oldest forms of law. But climate treaties are outdated the moment they are signed, because the climate is changing too quickly. And they don’t reflect the reality that climate change impacts — and opportunities to mitigate and adapt to climate change — are very different depending on location and context. (Sea level rise is not an issue in Mongolia; glacial melting does not plague Phoenix). The only viable way to make law and government is thus through relentless, highly structured and broadly collaborative local experimentation. This model, they noted, is neither “top down” nor “bottom up” but both at the same time.

“Our central aim is to reorient our current climate change regime away from failed efforts based on ex ante global consensus, and toward a system anchored in local and sectoral experimentalism and learning,” they wrote .

This local experimentalist mindset is emerging especially in the metro regions of countries that have advanced economies and histories of collaborative lawmaking and regulation.

Two places that best fit that description are Singapore, which was built on deep cooperation between government technocrats and industry, and Germany’s bigger cities.

Experimental law first emerged in West Germany during the 1950s as a pragmatic mechanism for the Länder, or states, to exploit their autonomy under the 1949 Basic Law. Faced with ideological divisions and a lack of national precedent for building a post-authoritarian society, municipal and state agencies used “trial clauses” to break legacy rules on welfare, housing and local administrative reorganizations without setting precedents or locking local governments into long-term mandates. The first official Experimentierklauseln allowed public schools to violate rigid curricular and education standards and test pedagogies, grading systems and models of comprehensive schools.

Experimental clauses fell out of fashion in the late 20th century but were revived for new challenges in the 21st century. In 2008, the Upper Saxony town of Bohmte, Germany , used an experimental clause to do something otherwise illegal: eradicate traffic lanes, street lines, traffic lights and stop signs to combat chronic speeding, utilizing a Dutch idea called shared space .

Over the last decade, climate change and advances in technology and transportation inspired so much local experimentalism that the German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action issued an official “Guide for Formulating Experimentation Clauses” in 2024. The guide runs 34 pages but contains three main rules: All experimental clauses must have an expiration date, a clear geographical or sectoral boundary, and rigorous evaluation.

Ask the federal ministry staff for a signature example, and you’ll hear about a Hamburg hospital that couldn’t get cancer tissue samples to a laboratory in time because of city traffic. The hospital wanted to use a drone instead, but German aviation regulations strictly forbid drones from flying “beyond the visual line of sight” of their operators over settled urban areas.

Instead of waiting years for federal airspace reform, Hamburg relied on experimental clauses to deviate from the federal Air Traffic Act for 18 months. During that time, the city-state established the U-Space Sandbox, a 30-square-kilometer experimental airspace over the Port of Hamburg.

Officials of the local and national governments worked with two German companies, Droniq and DFS Deutsche Flugsicheruntegration, to test the integration of drones with manned aviation. The experimentation eventually produced guidance and rules for a drone air traffic system, which are being incorporated into drafts of Germany’s federal U-Space Act.

“Climate treaties are outdated the moment they are signed, because the climate is changing too quickly.”

Living With Experimental Law

In Munich, I spent an evening inside one product of experimental law: an unusual new house at Goerzerstrasse 128, in the southeast neighborhood of Giesing. Munich, like so many cities, suffers from high housing prices and rents. The city held a competition for alternative solutions, and a self-organized housing syndicate won. It then used experimental clauses to deviate from strict German building codes.

The building was constructed with simple wood and cheap corrugated iron — what residents call “Favela-style” — and operates internally as a massive “shed flat.” The design is energy-efficient, and the roof captures rainwater in an underground cistern and feeds it directly back into the local groundwater table to combat drought. Read Noema in print.

The cost exceeded 3 million euros, drawn from public subsidies and private loans. But that’s cheap, given its scale. For now, 14 people — 13 adults and a six-year-old — share the open architecture, with frequent visitors. (A rock band was just leaving as I arrived.) The building is designed so it could be divided into at least nine separate apartments. While one-bedroom apartments in Munich rent for 1,700 euros a month, rent at Gorzer 128 is about 460 euros per person.

Gorzer 128 and other experiments helped inspire a national experimental clause called “Construction Turbo” (Section 246e of the German Federal Building Code), which allows municipalities to bypass existing planning standards until the end of 2030. The only unhappiness has come from neighbors who don’t like the building’s appearance (a jumble of metal and wood, quite different than the single-family craftsman homes on the street) and have been slow to engage with residents. Experimental law offers no cure for NIMBYism, at least not yet.

Beyond Gorzer 128, Munich’s experimental laws are most associated with efforts to transform streetscapes. A signal success is on the Kolumbusstraße, which a few years ago was a standard urban artery, lined with 120 concrete parking slots and choked with traffic.

Oliver May-Beckmann, who leads the MCube mobility cluster at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), says his group used an experimental clause to close the street to traffic for six months to create a Sommerstraße (Summer Street). Some drivers and residents complained to local officials. But because the project was a temporary and science-driven Reallabor , or real-world laboratory, politicians could push responsibility onto May-Beckmann and the scientists. “They’d say, ‘It’s just an experiment, let’s wait for the data,” he recalls.

For half a year , Kolumbusstraße became a green space where children could play, residents could spend time and new forms of mobility were tested. The transformation was deliberately temporary, and after six months, the street returned to its previous state. But the evaluation produced a striking result: 66% of residents supported making the changes permanent. Whether and how to turn the experiment into a lasting transformation is now a decision for the City of Munich.

MCube also used an experimental clause to test a car-sharing strategy in Nymphenburg, an affluent neighborhood that houses Munich’s botanical garden. For 20 years, Germany’s car industry — BMW, Mercedes, Sixt — had been testing different forms of free-floating vehicle-sharing to try to cut emissions, but it just put more cars on the street because people used shared vehicles on top of their own. In MCube’s test, 10 local families gave up their private cars for 18 months, and MCube bought five electric cars, plugged into charging stations in an underground garage, for the families to share. It was a closed group — the sharing was just between the 10 households, and you knew who had the car before you.

The families communicated with each other and shared the cars well. MCube also discovered that when people know a car is always nearby, they were willing to pay significantly more in regular payments for access than they would pay with one-off models. MCube is now working with both BMW and Sixt, the Bavaria-based rental car company, to spread the model around Germany. The experimental clause is still in effect and is being used to test alternative car-sharing models in three other Munich neighborhoods.

Experimental clauses offer flexibility but demand deep collaboration with business, governments and everyday people, May-Beckmann says. Take MINGA , a new project that plans to put autonomous buses on Munich’s streets this fall. (Minga is both the name for Munich in the Bavarian dialect and an acronym for Münchens Automatisierter Integrations-Nahverkehr mit Gesellschaftlicher Akzeptanz, or “Munich Automated Public Transport with Ridepooling, Solo Bus and Bus Platoons.”

The project, which uses driverless vehicles without a set schedule or route, is enabled by experimental clauses derived from 2021 amendments to Section 1i of the German Road Traffic Act. The German government is providing 13 million euros in funds. MAN, a German commercial vehicle manufacturer, built the buses. Technical University of Munich scientists have worked on the software, the public transport administration is preparing to run the buses, and the city of Munich plans to operate the service for two years under experimental clauses and then evaluate it. Finally, it requires people to sign up, primarily to bridge the “first-mile/last-mile” gap of getting people to public transit hubs.

Experimental clauses, at their best, create space and permission for systems integration. That’s nearly impossible in conventional governance, where decisions are made sequentially, and services and programs are added one by one.

“Our goal is transferring knowledge into prototypes and bringing those into real life,” says May-Beckmann. “It’s crucial in Europe that mobility innovation isn’t just about a new car; it’s about a system. How do you integrate autonomous driving, city development, climate change and energy? We get funding to have industry and public administration work for us as a system.”

“All experimental clauses must have an expiration date, a clear geographical or sectoral boundary, and rigorous evaluation.”

Experiments In Sunshine & Medicine

The desire to experiment with law is not exclusively German. Barcelona placed the 22@ Innovation District under experimental law to test drones. In the UK, Bethesda and other Welsh cities have employed experimental clauses for “ Sunshine Tariffs ” to encourage renewable energy use. South Korea carved out an experimental exception in its transportation laws to install a hydrogen-powered mobility system in Gyeongsangbuk-do. In Japan, the experimental mantle is carried by the “Future Design” movement, where citizens in towns like Yahaba wear differently colored robes to design infrastructure plans for future generations.

If democracy doesn’t have to be part of the legal equation, then East Asia might be the world’s leader. Singapore, the world leader in temporary regulations, has built a financial powerhouse by permitting banking and fintech experiments for decades. More recently, it has been applying experimentalism to medicine. An ongoing Health Sciences Authority experiment allows low- to medium-risk AI medical software to be used in public hospitals before formal registration. If the AI performs well for 12 months under clinician oversight, it can get an accelerated pathway to permanent approval.

More broadly, China and India have survived and prospered during rapid transitions by making experimentation a foundational principle of governance, often at the municipal or provincial levels.

In his 2024 book “Experimentalist Constitutions,” Peking University legal scholar Yueduan Wang details the Chinese government’s use of “experimental zones” to deviate from national law. In several areas, including green energy and mobility, municipalities have explicit legislative permission to try things. For example, the Shenzhen People’s Congress passed the 2025-2026 “Decision on Amending the Regulations of Shenzhen Special Economic Zone on Intelligent Connected Vehicles,” which allows fully driverless commercial taxis to bypass national safety standards.

India has embedded what it calls “regulatory sandbox” clauses directly into legislative updates. The Telecommunication Act of 2023 explicitly created a live testing environment that exempts companies from standard licensing fees to test 6G internet. Gujarat, where Narendra Modi served as chief before becoming national prime minister, is an epicenter of experimentation. It houses India’s first operational “smart city,” Gujarat International Finance Tec-City (GIFT City), between Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar, to test flexible financial regulations. Many of its startups use an “interoperable sandbox” to temporarily bypass rules on corporate governance, liquidity, capital minimums, reporting timelines and marketing as they test hybrid fintech products.

Experimental Enough For AI?

Despite successes in fintech, mobility and housing, it is unclear whether experimental law will be fast or flexible enough for the ethereal, borderless realm of artificial intelligence.

In Germany, companies working with AI complain that experimental law remained too slow and earthbound to keep up. Ironically, they blame the European Union’s attempts to “lead” on experimental law and AI for the failure.

In 2024, the EU embraced experimental law with its landmark AI Act. Article 57 of the AI Act included an explicit mandate for experimental law — every member state was required to establish at least one national “AI regulatory sandbox” by August 2026. But the mandate made the program politically divisive within several countries. In a dozen member states, including Germany and France, governments couldn’t even agree on which national agency or authority would establish their sandbox. The EU acknowledged the dysfunction this summer, pushing the deadline for a national AI mandate back a year to August 2027, via the AI Omnibus .

Few in Europe’s AI policymaking community expect to meet that deadline. The trouble goes beyond the EU’s slow bureaucracy. It’s hard to employ experimental law when you’re terrified of real impacts and results. Notably, the AI Act doesn’t require experimental deployment of AI regulation in the real world. As a result, those nations that are moving toward an AI regulatory sandbox are limiting experiments to theoretical exercises or purely legal assessments. But it’s impossible to create experimental laws for AI in the real world if you won’t experiment with AI in the real world.

In Munich, Till Klein, head of regulation at the non-profit “appliedAI Institute for Europe,” says that regulatory sandboxes that do exist for AI simply have too many restrictions to be useful. “Policymakers act like sandboxes will fix all the new rules,” says Klein. “But a sandbox is more like a sniper rifle than a shotgun; your experiment has to be precise for it to be meaningful.”

His colleague Demian Niemeyer, a lawyer and senior AI regulatory expert at appliedAI, sees the choke point as cultural. “People trained in law here are trained in a ‘Bismarck mindset,’” he says. “They are incredibly risk-averse. If you want to make something better and understand risks, you need a trial-and-error mindset.”

The paradox is that fear of applying experimental law to AI has left AI running free, well beyond law and regulation. Another fear also hamstrings experimental law: fear of regulatory capture.

That’s understandable, since effective experimental law requires regulators to collaborate closely with companies and stakeholders. Experimental law challenges the conception of regulation and law as walls between the watcher and the watched.

“The paradox is that fear of applying experimental law to AI has left AI running free, well beyond law and regulation.”

In 2024 and 2025, fear of capture stirred controversy and delayed the drafting of Germany’s federal Reallabore-Gesetz (Regulatory Sandboxes) Act, an attempt to go beyond experimental clauses on particular subjects and create a broader framework for experimental law.

The Social Democrats, left-wing groups and some scholars argue that broad authorization of experimental clauses risks turning into backdoor-lobbying channels for Big Tech and powerful corporations seeking exemptions from labor, safety and privacy laws. Most of the objections were AI-focused.

In response, the proposed law’s backers incorporated regulatorisches Lernen (regulatory learning) as a sandbox objective. When a project is approved under an experimental clause, the outcomes cannot remain hidden. The law requires continuous evaluation of the testing, and the resulting insights must be reported transparently. There are limited exclusions for genuine intellectual property.

The law also seeks to avoid narrow regulatory discussions between a company and a government agency via a “Regulatory Sandboxes Innovation Portal.” The portal is supposed to facilitate broad co-creation of law by connecting stakeholders from business, academia, public administration and civil society.

The legislation, renamed the Bundeserprobungsgesetz (Federal Proving Act), passed the Bundestag in late June. A second legislative body, the Bundesrat, would formally enact it as law in September. At the Munich Urban Colab, the immediate reaction was uncertainty. People would have to experiment with the new law and see.

stories.body:
What comes after the dissolution of the liberal world order.

Alden Young is an associate professor of history and global affairs at Yale University. He was a 2021-22 Berggruen Institute Fellow.

Muez Ali is an adjunct professor at Georgetown University in Qatar and honorary research fellow at University College London.

This work is supported by the Cross-Border Conflict Evidence, Policy and Trends (XCEPT) research program, funded by UK International Development. The views and opinions expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of the UK government.

Sudan has often served as a mirror for judging the health of the liberal world order because it has repeatedly been a laboratory for multilateral interventions to prevent atrocities and stabilize the humanitarian situation.

During the second Sudanese civil war, which stretched from 1983 to 2005, an estimated more than two million people died. In Darfur during the first decade of the 2000s, international observers estimated that 300,000 people died and another 2-3 million people were displaced.

At the time, finding a solution to Sudan’s conflicts was a priority for the United States and the coalitions it galvanized. For instance, Sudan’s second civil war came to an end only after intense mediation by the troika of the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway, as well as Sudan’s African neighbors, in 2005. The level of Western concern and diplomatic resources mobilized to intervene in Sudan’s conflicts in the early 2000s feels almost unimaginable today.

In the 2000s, Sudan hosted two massive UN peacekeeping missions : the more than 13-year-long African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur, which ended in 2020 and the more than six-year-long United Nations Mission in the Sudan, which ended in 2011. The goals of these missions were to prevent genocide in Darfur and to guarantee the implementation of the peace agreement ending the civil war between the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement/Army and the government in Khartoum. This mission, which included approximately 10,000 soldiers and numerous civilian authorities, ended with a referendum on the independence of South Sudan in 2011. A few months later South Sudan was welcomed by the international community as the newest country in the world.

It was in this context — of the international efforts to end Sudan’s civil wars and the resulting mass displacements — that South Sudanese diplomat Francis Mading Deng developed the idea of “ sovereignty as responsibility .” Deng served as the Special Representative of the United Nations Secretary-General on internally displaced persons from 1992 to 2004, and many experts credit Deng’s idea of sovereignty as responsibility as the intellectual genesis of the international principle of the Responsibility to Protect . The UN General Assembly’s adoption of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) principles in 2005 marked a high-water point for the legitimacy of the liberal world order. R2P, as formulated by Deng and others, tried to balance sovereignty as a state’s right to non-interference with the international community’s duty to ensure that a state protects the welfare of its own citizens.

Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm. The numbers are massive and stark, making it hard to comprehend the magnitude of the tragedy unfolding there. At least 14 million people have been internally displaced since the latest round of fighting in April 2023, according to the United Nations Refugee Agency. Meanwhile, there are at least 4.4 million Sudanese refugees who have fled the country, many to neighboring countries like Chad, Egypt and South Sudan, which can ill-afford to support this influx. Three years on, intense fighting persists in Sudan’s central region of Kordofan, in Darfur and in its southeastern Blue Nile state.

In one of the most widely discussed recent commentaries on the crisis in Sudan — a conflict often overshadowed despite its horrific violence by other wars — the American journalist and historian Anne Applebaum wrote that “no statistics can express the sense of pointlessness, of meaninglessness, that the war has left behind” after she reported from behind the lines of both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and their opponents, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). In the face of the physical destruction of cities like Khartoum, Applebaum declared the conflict the most nihilistic on Earth, writing with a tinge of hopelessness that “the liberal world order has already ended in Sudan, and there isn’t anything to replace it.”

In many ways, what is happening in Sudan represents the international community’s abandonment of the longstanding principles of the liberal world order, particularly by the West. Instead, Sudan has become the plaything for a wide array of actors stretching across the Middle East and Africa, to Russia and Ukraine, and as far afield as Colombia. After the Trump administration’s cuts to organizations like the U.S. Agency for International Development, even the commitment to prevent the spread of famine has declined. Applebaum ended her piece by lamenting that Sudan is now a victim of an anarchic, post-American world. A world that has yet to fully take shape in which “colonialism is long past, the Cold War has ended,” and the international order has irreparably broken down.

“Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm.”

But what is taking place in Sudan and elsewhere is not the emergence of anarchy; it is a return to precolonial patterns. Many observers have mistakenly assumed the former because of what the historian Richard Reid calls the “ foreshortening of African history ,” by which he means “the detachment of Africa’s turbulent present — and its recent past — from deeper patterns of both change and continuity.” Perhaps no country has suffered more from the reification of the colonial past by social scientists and modernizing elites alike than the Congo, once known as Zaire.

At the end of the 19th century, Henry Morten Stanley earned the name Bula Matari or the breaker of rocks, for “his feat of driving a caravan of porters bearing dismantled steamers over the torturous terrain between the Zaire River estuary and the vast navigable watercourses extending inward from Kinshasa.” As Zala Lusibu N’Kanza, the first woman to hold the position of minister in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, notes, “for all Bakongo the name of Bula Matari signified terror.” The precolonial was smashed in the wake of an ascendant and modernizing colonial and post-colonial state. For the founding generation of American political scientists like the late Crawford Young, the political, economic and social institutions of the precolonial period were left in ruins because they lacked the resilience to create an alternative to the modernizing state.

A Return To The Pre-Colonial Era

Despite the depths of the human tragedy playing out across northeast Africa — engulfing not only Sudan but South Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia and Somaliland — Applebaum’s post-American world is not just chaos. Clear patterns are emerging even amid the violence of state fracture. One of the clearest is the development of political and trade patterns resembling those of the pre-colonial era. The long dominance of the colonial state was not the result of smashing African societies, as American political scientists long suspected. Just as the chaos marring the post-colonial period is not a result of ethnic rivalries. Rather, the endurance of colonialism in countries like Sudan is a product of the legacies of its infrastructure.

The peculiar durability of the infrastructure built during European control of the Nile basin resulted from a set of historical conjunctures. In his new book, “The Alibi of Capital: How We Broke the Earth to Steal the Future on the Promise of a Better Tomorrow,” the political theorist Timothy Mitchell argues that around the turn of the 20th century a new ability to discount the future was invented. Mitchell considers this ability a political technology “derived from the fact that time can be controlled — by the construction of a political apparatus that will reliably capture and colonize the future.” While this sounds incredibly abstract, Mitchell goes on to explain that:

“That the scale and extension of transportation lines and energy networks, along with urban development, irrigation projects, and other immense schemes, depended not just on material durability but upon the durable arrangements of law, authority, compulsion, and justification.”

Sudan, though often imagined as a colonial backwater, was the site of one of the British Empire’s largest investments in industrial agriculture ever. The giant Gezira irrigated agricultural scheme, one of the only monuments to colonialism visible from outer space, was originally planned in the 1920s to irrigate more than a million acres. British officials spoke openly of the Gezira Scheme’s potential to be a second man-made Nile Delta, a giant cotton farm for the Empire. From the 1920s until the scheme ran into financial problems in the 1970s, the railways, dams, ports and even Sudan’s labor force were geared to serve this project, not to mention the country’s financial and economic infrastructure.

This changed in the 1990s as the oil sector rose to prominence, but even then, pipelines and refineries tended to be located according to patterns established during the colonial era. These patterns endured in part because irrigation canals and railways cut into the earth and were reinforced with steel, and because Sudan integrated into global financial markets through loans for investments backed by access to export markets. Originally, it was cotton, later crude oil and now gold.

The Fragile Liberal International Order

When the Princeton political scientist G. John Ikenberry wrote about the liberal international order, he remarked that, “there is an optimist assumption lurking in liberal internationalism that states can overcome constraints and cooperate to solve security dilemmas, pursue collective action, and create an open, stable system.” Yet Ikenberry also admits that the system’s collective nature was always more aspirational than practical. Ikenberry admits that since 1945 the United States has served as the owner and operator of this system and has been afforded special privileges and responsibilities. Applebaum describes the chaos that unfolds in Sudan once the United States is no longer willing to bear its historic burden. Read Noema in print.

“Clear patterns are emerging even amid the violence of state fracture. One of the clearest is the development of political and trade patterns resembling those of the pre-colonial era.”

But what if what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable? While cotton and crude petroleum are different commodities, the central state could largely control their export, either by managing production directly or by issuing licenses for production and sale to favored clients. The boom in gold exports from Sudan since 2013 is remarkable because of the state’s utter inability to control the trade. For Sudan, the tragedy is magnified by the almost 200% rise in gold prices during that period, meaning the Sudanese state lost out on this windfall due to incapacity and now war. Part of the challenge for Sudanese authorities is that artisanal gold production , unlike control of oilfields and pipelines or cotton irrigation, lacks the central infrastructural chokepoints the colonial and postcolonial state had become so adept at taxing.

The other dilemma for the Sudanese state is the regional collapse of the taboo against dealing with subnational actors. As a result, gold from the mines of Darfur often ends up in the souks of Dubai without ever passing through the central government. Similarly, Sudanese soldiers guarding the Saudi-Yemeni border can be hired and deployed without ever contracting with the SAF. The RSF, a paramilitary-slash-merchant company, carries out many of these transactions, managing large portions of Sudan on behalf of its investors.

Precolonial Patterns Return In Contemporary Guises

What looks like chaos reveals patterns. In the 3 ½ years since fighting broke out between the SAF and the RSF, new trade and military supply routes have become increasingly visible. During the first few decades following Sudan’s independence in 1956, most economic activity flowed from the provinces to Khartoum, then along the railroad lines to Port Sudan on the Red Sea. The government earned most of its revenue by taxing the imports and exports that followed this well-trodden route. During the first two years of fighting, the Rapid Support Forces controlled Khartoum and did everything in their power to break the old colonial trade route. During this time, Sudan’s government retreated to Port Sudan, and the RSF set up a rival capital in Nyala in southern Darfur.

Inadvertently, the war revealed older patterns of state formation from the 19th century. Sudan’s city of Suakin and its other Red Sea ports claimed allegiance to a distant Ottoman government and resisted incorporation into the Kingdom of Sennar, to say nothing of Darfur. Elites in Suakin often sought incorporation into the Ottoman province of the Hijaz or Aden on the Arabian Peninsula. This pattern threatened to repeat itself when Sudan’s government was again temporarily forced to relocate to Port Sudan after Khartoum fell in 2023.

But perhaps more dramatically, the war saw the re-emergence of old trade routes to the north, west and south of Darfur. With the SAF in control of Port Sudan, the RSF began to turn to the old trade routes across the desert, the most famous of which was the Darb El Arba’īn, or “40 Day Road,” leading from northern Darfur to Asyut in southern Egypt. Other trade routes led north into Libya, where the RSF is suspected to have established bases under the protection of the Libyan militia leader who rules the eastern part of the country, Khalifa Haftar. Similarly, the trading routes from southern Darfur into South Sudan have been reactivated to resupply the RSF. These routes often end in Uganda, Kenya and the Central African Republic. All outside the control of the center.

The new prominence of the old trade routes was capped by the declaration of TASIS , or the Sudan Founding Alliance, of a new government in April 2025, exactly two years after the outbreak of the war. Speaking from Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, TASIS leaders tried to solidify an alliance between the RSF, parts of the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), a militant group and political party, and the leadership of the Baggara confederation. The Baggara includes more than six million Arab and African people stretching from southern Kordofan to Lake Chad.

The RSF’s organization, founded in 2013 — with the Darfurian Arab family of its leader Muhammad Hamdan Daglo Musa at its center — itself echoes an episode from the late 19th century. The first is the creation of a private-merchant empire by al-Zubayr Rahma al-Mansur, usually known as Zubayr Pasha . Originally a lackluster merchant assistant for an Egyptian trader, by the 1860s Zubayr had established one of the largest merchant companies operating in what we today refer to as South Sudan.

His operations were described in a remembrance in the “Middle East Monitor” as such: “[He sent] men ‘through the lands of the Dinka, Jur and Bongo, the company reached the Golo, then living between the Kuru and Kpongo rivers.’ They purchased ostrich feathers and ivory for trade in Khartoum, Cairo and beyond.” By the 1870s, he had grown from a successful trader into the ruler of a territory often called Deim Zubayr, controlling a large area of present-day South Sudan’s Bahr al-Ghazal and Darfur with an army of some 12,000 soldiers, many of whom were enslaved. According to the historian Tsega Etefa , writing in the Journal of Oromo Studies:

“What if what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable?”

“By the late 1860s, al Zubayr was ‘the most prominent and successful of the merchant princes operating in the Bahr al-Ghazal.’ He traded in slaves and ivory; however, antislavery movements by Egyptian and European explorers in the Nile Valley began to put pressure on him. Therefore, ‘he arranged with the Baqqara tribes of southern Darfur for his slave caravans to pass through their territory northward, bypassing the Nile.’ Toward the end of the 1860s, ‘he attained the position of practically an independent ruler.’ The Egyptian government’s expeditionary force ‘was completely defeated by him, and the Egyptian authorities, realizing with what a commanding character they were confronted, made him Governor of the district.’”

Initially, Zubayr’s base was in the southern borderlands between Darfur and Bahr al-Ghazal. Darfur, as an independent political entity, was not conquered until 1874, when Zubayr’s forces achieved what the Ottoman-Egyptian armies of Muhammad Ali had been unable to do in 1821: conquering the Fur Sultanate at its capital of El Fasher. The parallels with the RSF appear to write themselves. These became particularly notable when the RSF took El Fasher after months of siege at the end of October 2025. In the process, the RSF captured the last major stronghold in Darfur and solidified their ability to resupply to the north through Libya and to the south across the expanse of South Sudan into East Africa.

Yet another echo of the 19th century was the emergence of Kordofan as a contested region. The armies of Muhammad Ali, de facto ruler of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, partially pacified the region in the decades after the 1821 invasion from Egypt, but could not maintain stable control. In many ways, this resembles the situation in Kordofan today, where cities like El-Obeid , with a population over 600,000, remain under frequent attack as rival forces contend to dominate the region. Still, the 19th-century echoes perhaps become clearest in the relative autonomy of the SPLM-N, a political party and militant group with its strongholds based in southern Kordofan.

The SPLM-N has been both a broker and spoiler for South Sudan since its secession in 2011. The flat plains were easily conquered, but the Nuba Mountains were very difficult to ultimately control. One faction, SPLM-N Al-Hilu, which mostly controls the areas around the Nuba Mountains in South Kordofan, sided with the RSF, while another faction, SPLM-N Agar, which controls parts of the Blue Nile state, has sided with the SAF.

In the process, the two groups have maintained the autonomy of the border regions between the RSF, SAF and South Sudan. A borderland organization more interested in preserving its own autonomy than in the outcome of the war has found itself operating on both sides of the conflict. In this way, they are implementing strategies with other surprising parallels in the past, such as the Kingdom of Taqali , a kingdom in the northeastern Nuba Mountains of Sudan that flourished between about 1780 and 1884, with relative autonomy that extended well into Sudan’s post-independence period until 1969.

Our research in the Sudan Collection at the University of Bergen in Norway shows that during the 19th century, Taqali leaders used a similar strategy of seeking protection and recognition from both the waning states of Darfur and Sennar — pledging vassalage to both simultaneously as they worked to maintain autonomy.

The breakdown of the Sudanese state we are witnessing today is also not random. Rather, along with the retreat of the liberal world order, we are witnessing the reappearance of political orders that last manifested themselves with such clarity in the 19th century. These patterns repeat because they are based on trade and political and economic linkages that do not rely on the infrastructure built during the colonial period. The durability of this infrastructure has decayed as the institutions of the liberal world order that maintained it have crumbled. In the place of the patterns of trade, infrastructure and political order that once felt like inevitable parts of the postcolonial world, we are witnessing the reappearance of the older routes of exchange.

For instance, we see the re-emergence of the Trans-Saharan routes, the trading routes into East and Central Africa and East-West connections across the Sahel and the Red Sea. In South Africa, there are calls to dissolve the Union of South Africa, which in 1910 joined the British Cape Colony with the independent Boer republics of the Transvaal and Free State as well as Natal. Yemen has been redividing for over a decade now in ways that are reminiscent of the 19th century, and of course Russian aggression has called into question the stability of eastern Europe’s borders.

These are just a few examples of how the stability that defined the second half of the 20th century cannot be taken for granted. As we think of what models might best explain statecraft after the liberal order, it increasingly makes sense to look at the 19th-century map as an example of political competition and shifting boundaries.

stories.body:
The luxury MV Odyssey ship slated for a years-long voyage around the world suspends operations amid high fuel prices

A luxury cruise ship that had embarked on a years-long voyage around the world was forced to suspend its operations and leave passengers stranded in Cambodia because of high fuel prices.

The ship, known as the MV Odyssey, had been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, Cambodian officials told the Associated Press . The ship has a 650-passenger capacity.

The Florida-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey, the company that operates the cruise line, said it was working with passengers on organizing “temporary living arrangements”. The cruise ship had begun its journey in Belfast in October 2024 for what was described as a “continuous voyage around the world”.

“Extraordinary increases in fuel costs have placed our current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure,” a statement on the company’s website said. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalization alternatives over the next 60 days.”

The ship is now docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with a departure date still unclear.

The price of fuel across the world has jumped since the start of the US war on Iran earlier this year. The ship’s operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800.

The strait of Hormuz, which transports much of the world’s oil, has effectively been closed since 28 February, the beginning of the war. Oil prices climbed to above $117 a barrel this month.

One resident on the ship, Randy Cassingham, wrote in a blogpost that he only discovered the cruise route’s cancellation after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship on Monday morning.

“It of course didn’t come from out of the blue: we’ve been well aware of problems,” Cassingham wrote. “It was a cascade of problems piling up on one another, from the business model to mistakes by management to the mentioned crisis in fuel cost and availability, and more.”

Pamela Reckamp, a 59-year-old resident of the ship, told NBC News that company officials on the ship had held a meeting last month where they asked cabin owners to help them raise $1m so the ship could depart Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.

“She said: ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp said. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”

Carol Larson, 69, lived on the ship for 18 months along with her sister, Crystal Lavering, 72, she told the Associated Press. Larson, who is from California, expressed hopes that the journey could still be salvaged because she said the decision to live at sea had improved her health.

Larson told the outlet that she bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, with additional monthly maintenance fees under a program that offered her the option of living onboard the ship for up to 15 years.

Larson blamed Donald Trump for the problems facing the ship and the suspended journey, as the war on Iran caused fuel costs to rise significantly. Despite the issues, however, Larson said she did not regret her investment.

“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk,” she said. “From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money’s worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising.”

stories.body:

It has been nearly five years since inflation crashed on to Australia’s shores, as a rebounding post-Covid economy collided with a world of constrained supply.

The global cost-of-living crisis – or affordability crisis, as the Americans call it – has shaped our world from 2022 onwards.

It was also the year that Russia invaded Ukraine, triggering the first of two global energy shocks.

The second energy shock, of course, arrived this February, when the United States and Israel decided to go to war with Iran.

It is in no small part due to the ongoing Middle East conflict, and the associated surge in fuel costs, that inflation in Australia jumped to 4.3% in the year to September.

While we remain focused on the dramas of 2026, it’s worth taking a longer-term view on how cost-of-living pressures have accumulated in recent years.

For example, fuel costs have risen by more than 20% in the past year, but over the longer term they have matched overall inflation (which is still a pretty big increase).

Our inflation explorer tracks all the categories included in the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ consumer price index.

Our interactive chart shows inflation has climbed 23% since the end of 2021.

But which goods and services have soared by more than that over recent years, and which haven’t?

You can explore the data at your own pace but here are some highlights.

Bills, bills, bills

No surprise that electricity is among the costs that have increased the most. Household power bills are up by 35% since the start of 2022.

The chart shows the zigzagging line as federal and state government subsidies have turned on and off. It is clear also that these subsidies, while welcome at the time, did nothing to change the upwards trend. Relatedly, gas is also up 49%.

Another cost that is hard to avoid is insurance, and the chart shows premiums have surged by 46% in nearly five years. Rental costs are 27% higher. Homebuilding costs are 36% higher.

Postal services are up 40%. Speaking of essentials, supermarket staples such as oil and eggs have increased by more than 40%, and bread, milk and fruit prices are up more than 30% in five years.

On the upside, chicken and vegetables have increased by less than inflation.

Not all bad news

The chart shows that, generally, the lowest price increases over recent years are for non-essentials.

Household items such as glassware, tableware and household utensils are actually cheaper. Electrical items, toasters and so forth, are on average no more expensive now than they were at the end of 2021.

Women’s clothing is just 7% more expensive, and men’s only 4%.

The biggest price decline has been in public transport fees – down 5%, presumably thanks to state and territory government decisions.

Perhaps the most surprising result is that childcare costs, while they have been rising of late, are only up 7% since the end of 2021.

stories.title: Tax thresholds remain unchanged - here's what it means for your pay
stories.summary: The point at which you start to pay tax, and the point where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax have been frozen for three more years.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 November 2025

Income tax thresholds, which have been frozen under successive chancellors, will stay at current levels until April 2031 as planned. But after that they are expected to start to rise again with inflation.

John Healey may not have mentioned the end of this policy in his Budget speech - after all, it is still some way off - but according to the documents released by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) the freeze, which has been shaving additional tax off people's take-home pay for the past five years, is scheduled to end.

The proportion of your income that is taken in tax will continue to go up over the next four years in line with decisions made in previous Budgets.

But then the personal allowance - the point at which you start to pay tax - and other thresholds, where you tip into paying a higher rate of tax, will rise again with inflation, meaning you keep more of what you earn.

Freezing thresholds is often dubbed a stealth tax because, unlike raising the headline rates, it is not as obvious on your payslip.

It has been a useful way for chancellors from Rishi Sunak onwards to raise more money to help pay for things like defence, the NHS, schools and support for the sick, disabled and the elderly.

The amount of extra money brought in by freezing tax thresholds has risen steadily every year, and is due to reach £58bn by 2030-31, more than the UK government spends on transport and not far off current defence spending.

Who is affected by frozen thresholds?

They hit you hardest if your income is close to one of the tax thresholds, but anyone who gets a pay rise is affected, as long as you earn enough to pay tax. Only people earning under £12,570 - the personal allowance threshold - pay no income tax.

By 2031 an extra 6.8 million people will be paying tax who wouldn't have if the personal allowance had not been frozen, the OBR calculates.

The state pension is currently just below the personal allowance threshold, and pensioners looked set to be drawn into paying tax from next April, when the basic state pension rises to £13,036.

However, the chancellor is putting in place a new separate Pension Tax Allowance, which will ensure that low-income pensioners, with income up to the value of the full new state pension, will not pay income tax .

The personal allowance threshold is set for the whole UK, so people in Scotland will also be affected, although other tax bands there vary , external .

National Insurance Contributions (Nics) are levied according to the same thresholds.

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published 4 hours ago

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance Published 4 hours ago

How does it work?

Wages usually go up year-on-year to cover the rising cost of living. Normally tax thresholds would also be raised in line with rising prices. Currently that isn't happening - the thresholds have been "frozen" at 2021 levels.

So, as your pay rises, a bigger proportion of it ends up above the threshold where you start to pay tax.

If the personal allowance had risen with inflation over the last five years, you would now be able to take home the first £16,070 of your salary without paying any income tax. Instead you pay 20% on anything you earn above £12,570.

Will I pay the higher rate?

As incomes rise, frozen thresholds also mean more and more people are dragged into the higher, 40%, tax bracket.

An extra 5.4 million will be higher rate taxpayers by 2031, thanks to the freeze, according to the OBR.

If thresholds had risen with inflation you would have had to be earning £64,470 this year before you tipped into the higher tax bracket.

As it is, with thresholds frozen at 2021 levels, you pay the higher rate on anything you earn over £50,271.

If you were already earning more than the threshold and you get a pay rise, a bigger proportion of your earnings will be taxed at the higher rate.

Almost one in four taxpayers will pay some of their tax at the higher rate by 2031, according to the government's official forecaster.

The same principle - that rising income can push you into a new tax bracket - applies to the additional, 45%, rate that is charged on a person's income over £125,140.

Will I be better off after 2031?

Wages have risen sharply to keep up with inflation in recent years, making the impact of the first five years of this policy quite noticeable, and that is set to continue.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) says if Healey had unfrozen the personal allowance this week, instead of keeping it in place until 2031, basic rate taxpayers would have saved up to £198 in tax a year.

Higher rate taxpayers would save £395 a year.

However, for people in the middle of the earnings range, a cut to Nics introduced in 2024 has offset the higher income tax bill.

How much of a difference "unfreezing" thresholds will make in four years' time depends on how fast wages are going up at that point.

There is no fundamental principle at stake, no point that is the "right" level for tax thresholds. Before the financial crisis the personal allowance was much smaller than today, and it was allowed to grow until the pandemic hit. Even in 2031 you'll be able to take home a bigger proportion of your earnings before income tax than you could back in 2008.

stories.title: Burnham rules out early general election in next 12 months
stories.summary: The prime minister has denied speculation from some opposition parties that he will go to the country in spring 2027.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The prime minister was asked about speculation from the Tories and Reform UK

Published 2 hours ago

Andy Burnham has ruled out an early general election in the next 12 months, after opposition parties suggested one would be called.

The next UK general election must be held by August 2029, and there has been speculation that the prime minister is preparing for an earlier poll.

Asked directly if he would call a snap election within the next year, the prime minister told broadcasters: "I don't know how many times I've done this now but yes, I can rule out calling a general election in the next 12 months."

He said he was focusing on people over the Labour Party, adding: "I'm not thinking about myself. I'm not thinking about my own party and its prospects."

Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch suggested Burnham may go to the country early.

She said the Conservative Party was "coming back" after it slumped in popularity at the end of 14 years in government, telling BBC South East: "This is an era of political volatility and multi-party politics."

She added: "I do think Andy Burnham is going to call an election sooner than he is saying... all the policies he announced are for after an election."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said in September he believed there would be an election "next spring".

"I believe there must be a general election because Andy Burnham has no mandate - the messiah without a mandate, we deserve a general election on who continues to govern this country."

Burnham was elected MP in June after the Makerfield by-election, before securing the Labour Party leadership and becoming prime minister after Sir Keir Starmer lost the support of Labour MPs and quit Downing Street.

He has since outlined a number of ambitions , which has led some to question whether he will try to secure a fresh mandate before 2029.

One of these issues is Brexit, where Burnham has said he wants an "honest conversation" about the UK's future relationship with the EU.

On Wednesday, he promised to stick to the red lines in his party's 2024 manifesto on EU freedom of movement, the single market and customs union "for the whole of this Parliament".

The current Parliamentary term runs until the next general election.

Burnham has repeatedly denied he is seeking a snap poll. He told broadcasters on Wednesday: "We've got a 10-year plan to come, and that will inform the spending review next year. These are my priorities, not looking at our own internal party political advantage."

stories.title: Healey tells departments to make 1% cuts to fund defence
stories.summary: The reduction in public spending will go towards paying for the Defence Investment Plan.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Members of the Finnish army and British army on a training exercise on Nato's border with Russia

Published 28 October 2026, 17:32 GMT

Chancellor John Healey has told every government department to find 1% cuts in their capital budgets to fill a £4.7bn hole in the funding of the Defence Investment Plan.

The reductions come on top of the 1% cuts departments were asked to make earlier this year in order to pay for the initial £10.3bn of the plan's overall £15bn price tag.

The plan boosted defence spending; however the chancellor continues to come under pressure to explain how he will meet a further target of spending 3% of national income on defence by 2030.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the chancellor of only offering "a plan to have a plan" adding: "I bet [Vladimir] Putin's really scared now."

Setting out his Budget, Healey hinted that meeting that goal would require further cuts, telling MPs it would involve "looking hard at public spending".

He said he would set out how the UK would reach the 3% target by 2030, as well as 3.5% of GDP by 2035, at next year's spending review.

Government departments have yet to decide what will be cut from their capital budgets.

Capital budgets are focused on long-term investments, rather than day-to-day spending. For example, earlier this year, when departments had to make capital budget cuts to fund the initial defence spending rise, a number of major road improvement schemes were scrapped .

Badenoch criticised Healey for not using his Budget to explain how he would boost defence funding to 3%.

"He is the man who is making our country less safe. He has failed his own test. This is on him, and no one will ever forget," she said.

The Conservatives have previously urged the government to pay for defence by making cuts to the welfare budget.

Nato secretary general Mark Rutte said the UK was on "a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato Allies in The Hague - to ensure we're all investing what's needed to remain ready & able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security".

Chair of the Commons defence committee - and Labour MP - Tan Dhesi said "some of the key decisions on defence spending have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review".

He added: "There is a cost to inaction. Investment in our nation's defence and security cannot be kicked into the long grass."

Former Nato secretary general Lord Robertson told the BBC the Budget was "pretty good news for defence generally" but warned there would be "battles ahead with the spending departments" to reach the 3% target.

Earlier this year, Healey resigned as defence secretary, accusing the then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer of not providing enough money to keep the UK safe.

In a scathing resignation letter, he specifically emphasised his belief in the importance of reaching a 3% target by 2030.

Now chancellor, Healey told the House of Commons on Wednesday: "At the spending review next year, I confirm that I will set out the details of how we will meet our Nato commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for 3% in 2030.

"And today, I am getting work under way to get there in a fiscally sustainable way."

In addition to looking at public spending, Healey said he also wanted to use "more innovative financing alongside the private sector and our international allies".

The chancellor said this would include:

starting treaty negotiations with Finland, Poland and Netherlands to set up a "multilateral defence mechanism" which would allow allies to share resources

increasing the amount of private investment in defence through public-private partnerships

directing the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to put £5bn into "defence, dual-use technology and sovereign capability"

The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that the UK government's target to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 will cost £35bn.

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: "Increasing investment in defence companies may contribute to the target but it is unclear how much this will lead to an increase in UK defence capabilities.

"There is much further to go to get to 3% of GDP on defence and it is hard to believe that this government will want to get there without topping up spending totals."

Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role Published 16 October

Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump calls latest strikes a 'disgrace' Published 16 October

Burnham treads carefully with Zelensky visit, balancing Trump and Ukraine Published 14 October

In his Budget speech, Healey also announced £10bn of economic and military support for Ukraine, in the form of loans and export guarantees.

The funding includes £5.5bn of loans through World Bank guarantees and a grant contribution to the World Bank International Development Association's crisis facility.

A further £3bn will be made available to Ukraine through loans facilitated by UK Export Finance, a government export credit agency.

Healey told the House of Commons that the week had started with Russia launching a "brutal ballistic missile attack" and that the extra money would send "a clear message to Moscow".

He said that when he told the Ukrainian leader about the additional support in a phone call, President Volodymyr Zelensky had said: "You've made my day."

Later on social media, Zelensky welcomed the money, saying: "Every step to strengthen Ukraine brings Russia closer to realising that it must end this war of its own making."

The money comes on top of the UK's pledge to provide Ukraine with £3bn of military support until at least 2030-31.

Published 28 September 2026

Chancellor John Healey has set out the government's tax and spending plans in his Budget – the first since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

Here is a summary of the main points.

LIVE: Follow all the Budget coverage

One-off £100 payment for up to 20 million households in council tax bands A-D in England to help deal with rising energy bills, with equivalent funding for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland

Standing charges – fixed daily fees customers pay regardless of usage – to be removed from household gas bills in England, Scotland and Wales, with costs added to the unit rate instead

VAT cut on electricity bills extended to July

A green levy - the Gas Shipper Obligation to fund hydrogen projects - to be removed from energy bills and put on to general taxation

Freeze on fuel duty extended again to July

Import taxes to be removed on more than 100 food products, including gherkins and marmalade, as well as kerosene and fertilisers

A 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work made permanent, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that distance

A new scheme taking 25% off electricity bills for 10,000 energy-intensive businesses to launch in April, with payments backdated for energy costs this year

From April 2027, landlords will face a further 2% in income tax on rental profits

An extra 2% tax on income from savings and property rental from April

Amount people can put into tax-free cash Isas (Individual Savings Accounts) to remain at £20,000 a year, with plans to lower the limit to £12,000 for under-65s scrapped

Surcharge banks pay on their profits to rise from 3% to 6% for 15 months, starting in January

Threshold at which High Street shops start paying business rates in England to be increased from £12,000 to £18,000, meaning businesses would pay no rates on properties with a rateable value below this level

Adult games centres and vape shops will no longer qualify for certain business rates relief

Taxes on gambling machines with stakes over £1 to rise from 20% to 25%

Online marketplaces like Amazon, eBay and Temu to be made responsible for collecting VAT owed by sellers using their platforms

New, flat-rate state pension to rise by £488 a year from April – equivalent to 3.9% - under the triple lock policy , with old basic state pension to rise by £374.40

A new tax-free allowance for low-income pensioners, to ensure those with income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax

Legal minimum wage to rise by 3.9% in April

Unpaid carers will no longer lose their entire Carer's Allowance if they earn more than £204 a week after tax, with a taper rate introduced instead

Parental pay extended to self-employed fathers and parents in same-sex couples

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you Published 4 hours ago

A further £432m has been added to the initiative to end rough sleeping by Christmas

New scheme to help first-time buyers in England purchase a home, offering government-backed loans to households earning less than £110,000 , or £140,000 inside London

A new First Time Buyer ISA to be introduced from April 2029, to replace the Lifetime ISA and help people save a deposit for their first home

Lifetime ISA holders buying a property above the £450,000 cap will pay a reduced withdrawal charge of 20%, down from 25%

An extra £1bn for social and affordable housing in England , taking total funding for the 10-year programme to more than £40bn

An extra £432m for a programme aimed at giving every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas

All business rates to be retained locally by the end of the decade, with mayors to keep 20% of revenue from next year

A share of income tax receipts to go to mayors from 2028

Regional bodies and mayors in England to get greater powers over spending, starting with £285m next year for things like housing, transport and High Streets

Government to work with mayors to design a £1.5bn borrowing facility, enabling investment in larger projects

The chancellor promised an uplift in defence spending by 2030

Defence Investment Plan to be fully funded through a further 1% cut to capital budgets of other government departments , after Sir Keir Starmer only committed £10.3bn for the £15bn plan

Details of how the government will meet a Nato commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 to be set out at next year's Spending Review, with a target date for 3% in 2030

Extra £10bn of economic and military support for Ukraine

More than £600m of investment in projects related to artificial intelligence (AI), including an extra £120m for the UK's AI Security Institute and £100m for a national AI Biosecurity Lab

A £7m fund to explore a possible future bid to hold the Olympics and Paralympics in northern England

Fund to tackle misogyny in schools, at work and in communities to get £15m

Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) predicts the UK economy will grow by 1.2% this year, up from a previous estimate of 1.1%

Growth then expected to slow to 1% next year, a downgrade from the watchdog's previous forecast of 1.6%, before lifting back to 1.6% in 2028

stories.title: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
stories.summary: The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the Brexit deal at a summit in Brussels next month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Prime Minister's Questions focused on Andy Burnham's Brexit stance

Published 28 October 2026, 13:38 GMT

Andy Burnham has insisted there is "no confusion" over his position on the European Union, as he criticised the UK's current deal with the bloc.

The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the deal, which was ratified in 2020, at a summit in Brussels next month.

He denied he had shifted his stance since the Makerfield by-election when he promised not to "re-run" the Brexit debate . Earlier this week, he suggested he could call a referendum on the UK returning to EU freedom of movement, before No10 appeared to backtrack .

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday of failing to "respect" the 2016 Brexit vote.

Badenoch said Burnham had created confusion and asked if he wanted a referendum on rejoining the EU.

"There is no confusion at all," Burnham told MPs.

"The government has a collectively agreed position, which I have set out today.

"It is entirely consistent with everything that I've said, including in the by-election.

"The red lines in our manifesto, including on freedom of movement, will stay in place firmly for the whole of this Parliament."

Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

Freedom of movement allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country.

It is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market, which enables goods, services and people to move freely between EU member states.

Badenoch accused Burnham of having "opened his mouth without engaging his brain" over freedom of movement during "the chancellor's big week" as the Budget is unveiled .

No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion Published 2 days ago

Burnham pledges not to 're-run' Brexit arguments Published 18 May

Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days Published 1 day ago

Recalling the mood in Parliament and the country in 2017 when the current Brexit deal was being fought over, Badenoch said: "We do not want to go through that again - the country was paralysed.

"It was miserable, regardless of which side of the debate you were on."

Burnham said Badenoch was "speaking the truth" here and the country had suffered from low growth and insufficient control on migration as a result of a "harder Brexit than what was promised" in the 2016 referendum.

"Where I am focused is getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility, and I will lead from this despatch box over the next few weeks," Burnham said.

At a summit in Brussels on 20 November, Burnham will push options for a reset of relations with the bloc on issues such as youth mobility, food, drink, energy and cooperation on illegal immigration.

Burnham's comments at Prime Minister's Questions came as a letter emerged addressed to his Cabinet ministers, asking them to be "aligned and disciplined" around the summit.

"It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process," he wrote in a letter on Wednesday.

He said he hoped the summit led to "some important, concrete steps" and he would set out the next steps "to consider the UK's long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan".

"Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote," he said.

"Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality."

Any "fundamental change" to this relationship "would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next Parliament," he added.
